EFA1
IF, IFS and logical tests
Watch first
1. 5 Advanced Tips on how to use IF formula in Excel that will SURPRISE you
Earlier package watch range: 0:00-4:45. Stop manually at each listed endpoint. Topic assignment retained; chapter
boundaries and full playback have not been reverified in this review. See simple IF, nested/IFS, then the
multi-condition section that supports AND/OR logic before reproducing the workbook task.
Pause to connect the demonstration to the example below. Use the printed stop time when a bounded range is
given; longer recordings remain available for reference.
Why this matters
A spreadsheet can label an undelivered order "On Time" if you compare a blank date with a real
date. Before calculating, decide which records have enough information. The business rule is the
sentence; the formula is its implementation.
Open P-EFA1_IF. Rows 11-16 contain one record per Order ID. Columns B and C are promised and
actual dates; D is a score. This exercise has no cancellation field, so do not invent cancelled
orders. The supplied dates are valid date-only values; a missing actual date means the result is
unknown.
Words before we use them
Word
Plain meaning
Logical test
A comparison returning TRUE or FALSE
Branch
The answer chosen after a test
Boundary
An exact cutoff, such as 90
AND
Every condition must be true
OR
At least one condition must be true
Follow with me once
The rule is: missing actual date -> Missing date; otherwise actual on or before promised -> On
Time; otherwise Late. In E11 enter:
=IF(C11="","Missing date",
IF(C11<=B11,"On Time","Late"))
This is one formula; line breaks only help it fit on the page. Fill E11 down to E16. IF takes a test,
an answer when true and an answer when false. The outer test prevents the blank in C14 from
being treated as an early delivery. Equality is on time: O-101 has the same promised and actual
date.

For this fictional score, 90-100 is A, 75-89 is B, 60-74 is C and 0-59 is D. Scores are supplied as
numbers in that range. In F11 enter and fill through F16:
IFS stops at the first true test. Testing >=60 first would incorrectly catch a score of 95. TRUE is
the final default. If IFS is unavailable, use the equivalent nested IF:
Check O-102 at 90 and O-106 at 75. Both belong to the higher band at equality. In G11:G16 write
your checks; H can hold short explanations. Before applying this pattern to new data, validate
missing, nonnumeric and out-of-range scores separately.
Try it yourself
Retry_Data!A5:D9 contains the commission case. Put the eligibility result in D6:D9. Only East
with Sales >=50000 qualifies. Write the rule first, then use IF and AND. OR would accept East
below the cutoff or a non-East record above it; that is a different rule.
Save the attempt. Review EFA1 in the protected answers. Close it and change the second sales
value from 50000 to 49999. Predict which result changes before recalculating; restore the value
afterward. Also test the score formula with 60 then 59 in a working copy and restore the score.
You are ready when you can explain the blank-date guard and both boundaries.

EFA2
SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and AVERAGEIFS
Watch first
1. Best Excel Formulas in an hour - Beginner to PRO Masterclass
Earlier package watch range: 1:51-8:28. Stop manually at each listed endpoint. Topic assignment retained; chapter
boundaries and full playback have not been reverified in this review. See COUNTIFS, SUMIFS and AVERAGEIFS with
multiple criteria before building a cell-driven analyst report.
Pause to connect the demonstration to the example below. Use the printed stop time when a bounded range is
given; longer recordings remain available for reference.
A question needs a precise population
Open P-EFA2_ConditionalAgg. There are 23 transactions in A11:G33, with headers on row 10.
Row 34 begins instructions: it is not data. Sales are fictional INR amounts; Delivery Days are
elapsed days for each transaction. J11:J15 contain the report inputs.
SUMIFS adds values from records satisfying all criteria. COUNTIFS counts matching records.
AVERAGEIFS averages a numeric field for the matching records. A criteria range is the column
you test; a criterion is what it must satisfy. The ranges must align row by row.
Build three different answers
J17 answers total Sales for the selected Region AND Category, across every supplied date. Enter:
The first range contains numbers to add. The next pairs are field, condition. East AND Furniture
matches T001 and T013. Their 12000 + 32400 = 44400. Looking only at East would include more
categories and answer a different question.
J18 answers the count in the selected Region with Sales at least the threshold, across all supplied
dates:
The & joins the operator text ">=" to the number in J15. With East and 25000, T009, T013, T017
and T021 qualify: four transactions. The wording is "at least", so equality qualifies.
J20 answers average Delivery Days for the selected Region from J13 through J14, including both
dates:
These inputs are date-only, without times. For timestamp data, a safer inclusive-day design uses
an exclusive next-day endpoint; do not assume this exact comparison includes every time on an
end date. With the supplied East window, the six day values are 1, 5, 1, 5, 1, 5: average 3 days.
Category is intentionally absent from this third question.

Check without trusting the formula
Select A10:G33, turn on Data > Filter, filter East and Furniture, and list the visible IDs and sales
separately in J24:J28. Clear the filters afterward. SUMIFS still includes matching hidden records;
filtering alone does not change its criteria. Do not call the result a visible-row subtotal.
Independent task and repair
Close the examples. Change Region to West, Category to Office, threshold to 30000 and the end
date to =DATE(2026,2,28). Keep the start date =DATE(2026,1,1). Predict which question each
input affects. Rebuild the three formulas if necessary and manually validate one answer. Save
before opening EFA2's solution.
For a further retry, use Region Central, which has no records. SUMIFS and COUNTIFS return 0; the
unguarded average returns #DIV/0! because there are no observations. Zero days would invent
an observed average. Restore the original inputs. If you get an unexpected zero or error, check
spelling, types, criteria and identical range lengths before wrapping anything in IFERROR.

EFA3
Cleaning text while preserving
meaning
Watch first
1. Data Cleaning in Excel - 10 Tricks (Beginner to PRO)
Earlier package watch range: 1:17-8:49. Stop manually at each listed endpoint. Topic assignment retained; chapter
boundaries and full playback have not been reverified in this review. See Flash Fill/Text to Columns/duplicate and
cleaning patterns, then return to the safer raw-preserving helper-column workflow.
Pause to connect the demonstration to the example below. Use the printed stop time when a bounded range is
given; longer recordings remain available for reference.
Raw values and approved display values
Open P-EFA3_Cleaning. A11:D17 contains seven records and six distinct Customer IDs. The
expected grain is one customer per ID; the second C003 needs investigation. Several customers
live in Delhi. A repeated city is not a duplicate customer.
The exercise approves ordinary-space trimming, title case for the display Name/City and
uppercase Status. These are display conventions, not legal-name corrections. Keep A:D
untouched. TRIM removes leading/trailing ordinary spaces and repeated internal ordinary
spaces. CLEAN handles many control characters; neither function fixes every Unicode space or a
misspelled place.
Follow with me
In E11:H11 enter these formulas, then fill down through row 17:
E11: =PROPER(TRIM(B11))
F11: =PROPER(TRIM(C11))
G11: =UPPER(TRIM(D11))
E11 becomes Riya Sharma, F11 Delhi and G11 ACTIVE. The source spaces remain visible in the
formula bar when you select B11. COUNTIF asks how many times this row's ID occurs in the fixed
ID range. Both C003 rows return TRUE, not only the later occurrence. The rows may represent a
repeated export or conflicting source records; a flag does not authorise deletion.
Do not use PROPER on an identifier or on a company acronym without approval. It would turn an
acronym into title case. Flash Fill (Data > Flash Fill, often Ctrl+E) infers a pattern from examples
and writes values. It does not create a persistent formula rule. If you use it on a disposable copy,
change the input afterward to see why the output must be checked again.

Try it yourself
Retry_Data!A13:G17 holds four supplier records. Preserve A:C. This case allows
trimming/uppercase for the City display, but names must retain their case because they may be
legal names. Use D for a trimmed name, E for a normalised city, F for the issue, and G for your
proposed action. "DELH1" is suspicious, not an approved spelling of DELHI. Two different supplier
IDs can share a city. A repeated Supplier ID must be flagged even if its display fields match.
Save, then read the matching worked answer. Close it and replace the suspicious city with " pune
" in a second attempt after recording that this is an owner-confirmed correction for the exercise.
Recalculate the helper and keep the original attempt. Your row count remains four; changing a
label does not remove a record. Explain why automatic deletion or guessing a spelling would
have been unsafe.

EFA4
Text extraction and dates you can
calculate with
Watch first
1. Chandoo - Important Excel text functions (instructor video)
Optional visual, no verified bounded range. Linked by the instructor on the text-functions article and the destination
title corroborated on 17 September 2026. Focus on LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LEN and FIND; the book separately teaches
the date task. Full playback not checked.
2. Chandoo - 6 Essential TEXT functions + Date & Time values
Text reference, not a video. Optional visual/reference reinforcement for text extraction and Excel date serial
thinking.
3. Chandoo - Date & Time values in Excel
Text reference, not a video. Reinforces how Excel stores and works with dates.
Pause to connect the demonstration to the example below. Use the printed stop time when a bounded range is
given; longer recordings remain available for reference.
Characters are not the same as numbers
Open P-EFA4_Text_Dates. The four invoice codes follow PREFIX-YEAR-SUFFIX, such as
INV-2026-00481. A prefix is the first part; a suffix is the last part. LEFT and RIGHT select
characters; MID selects from a given character position; LEN counts characters. FIND is
case-sensitive and SEARCH is not. Both return a position, and fail when the requested text is
absent.
An identifier ending 00481 is usually text so its zeros survive. Only convert it to 481 when you
explicitly need a numeric sequence. You are extracting a code, not calculating money.
Work through the first record
In C11 enter =LEFT(A11,3). In D11 enter =RIGHT(A11,5), keeping its output as text. This returns
INV and 00481. =MID(A11,5,4) returns 2026; =LEN(A11) returns 14 and =FIND("-",A11) returns
4. Confirm those positions on the actual code before filling C:D through row 14.
Dates are stored as numbers and displayed using date formatting. ISNUMBER tests the stored
type. It does not prove that an arbitrary number is a sensible business date; the source contract
must also establish its meaning. Here B11:B13 are valid supplied dates. B14 is the literal text
"08/22/2026 text", so formatting it as a date will not repair it.
Use the fixed reporting date 22 August 2026. Put these formulas in E11:I11 and fill to row 14:
E11: =IF(ISNUMBER(B11),YEAR(B11),"Investigate")
F11: =IF(ISNUMBER(B11),MONTH(B11),"Investigate")
G11: =IF(ISNUMBER(B11),EOMONTH(B11,0),"Investigate")
H11: =IF(ISNUMBER(B11),DATE(2026,8,22)-B11,"Investigate")
I11: =IF(ISNUMBER(B11),"Numeric date","Review text")

Format G as dd-mmm-yyyy. Keep E/F/H as whole numbers. For the first record, 15 January to 22
August is 219 elapsed days; the start day is not counted as day one. TODAY() would change with
the day you study, which would defeat a fixed expected answer.
Independent extraction with a broken pattern
Retry_Data!A21:I24 has three service codes. The approved pattern is uppercase SV- followed by
exactly five digits. Inspect each of these three codes and record Valid or Investigate in H; this is a
manual check that you must repeat if a code changes. Return the two-character prefix in C and
five-character suffix in D only for a valid pattern; otherwise write "Investigate". Do not blindly
extract from SRV-0125. Use E for Year, F for Month End, G for days to the fixed date and I for the
separate date-type explanation.
The text date "01/02/2026" is ambiguous without a source locale. Leave it unresolved in your
first attempt. After review, the case owner confirms DD/MM/YYYY. In a second attempt write
=DATE(2026,2,1) as a separate resolved value and compute days; do not overwrite the original
evidence. Explain why changing its display format alone was insufficient.

EFA5
Lookups with a key you can trust
Watch first
1. 10 Advanced XLOOKUP Tips & Tricks
Earlier package watch range: 1:15-4:18. Stop manually at each listed endpoint. Topic assignment retained; chapter
boundaries and full playback have not been reverified in this review. See XLOOKUP syntax/basic/multi-column
behavior before practicing key uniqueness and Not Found controls.
2. Microsoft XLOOKUP reference and embedded visual
Official function/compatibility reference, with an embedded visual player. No verified watch range. Exact match and
first-match behavior explain why the key check matters.
Pause to connect the demonstration to the example below. Use the printed stop time when a bounded range is
given; longer recordings remain available for reference.
A lookup attaches an attribute
Open Products and P-EFA5_Lookups. Products!A6:D13 has one record for each of eight Product
IDs. Transactions are in A11:C15 of the practice sheet: one row per Txn ID. Product ID may
repeat across transactions. It must identify exactly one master record before you attach a price
or category.
Check the master first: in Products!F5 type Key Count, then F6 =COUNTIF($A$6:$A$13,A6), filled
through F13. Every result should be 1. A lookup returning a plausible first match does not prove
the key is unique.
Follow with me
On P-EFA5_Lookups, put these in D11:F11 and fill through row 15:
D11: =XLOOKUP(B11,Products!$A$6:$A$13,
Products!$B$6:$B$13,"Not Found",0)
E11: =XLOOKUP(B11,Products!$A$6:$A$13,
Products!$C$6:$C$13,"Not Found",0)
F11: =XLOOKUP(B11,Products!$A$6:$A$13,
Products!$D$6:$D$13,"Not Found",0)
The parts are: key to find, fixed key range, aligned return range, missing result and exact-match
mode 0. P101 returns Desk, Furniture and 12500. In H11 use
=IF(COUNTIF(Products!$A$6:$A$13,B11)=1,"Matched","Investigate"). In G11 use
=IF(H11="Matched",C11*F11,"Investigate"). Fill G:H down. A missing or duplicated master key
remains a problem even if another formula displays a value.
L001 has three units, so 3 x 12500 = 37500. P999 has no master match. Do not replace its price
with zero and call the total complete. SUM can ignore text markers: report the known-value
subtotal and unresolved-row count together.
FOUR-COURSE SYSTEM  /  2026
C1 / M02  /  LEARNER BOOK
Astra-parity study edition 2.0  |  Video, explanation, practice, proof

If your Excel does not support XLOOKUP
Use =IFNA(VLOOKUP(B11,Products!$A$6:$D$13,2,FALSE),"Not Found") for Product; use column
number 3 for Category and 4 for Price. FALSE requests an exact match. VLOOKUP requires the
key in the leftmost column of its range. Another exact pattern is
INDEX(return_range,MATCH(key,key_range,0)). These are compatibility routes; the uniqueness
and missing-key checks still apply. IFNA handles missing matches, while broad IFERROR can hide
unrelated failures.
Try it yourself
Retry_Data!A28:C31 is a Department master; A35:F38 contains employees. Enrich C:D with
Department and Cost Centre, E with the matching-key count and F with an action. D99 must
remain unresolved. Verify a matched row by reading the master yourself. After review, duplicate
D20 in a separate working copy with a conflicting Cost Centre. Explain why you must stop rather
than accept XLOOKUP's first result. Restore the master before continuing.

EFA6
Handle errors without hiding the
cause
Watch first
1. Chandoo - Excel Formula Errors: Understand and Debug Them
Text reference, not a video. Optional reference for recognizing error types; the lesson controls when an error may
be handled versus repaired.
Pause to connect the demonstration to the example below. Use the printed stop time when a bounded range is
given; longer recordings remain available for reference.
An error can protect the reader
Open P-EFA6_Errors. The four cases in rows 11-14 describe different problems. Put a handling
decision in F, your proposed formula or repair in G and the reason in H. This is a diagnosis
exercise: a blank report is not automatically a better report.
Signal
What to investigate
#DIV/0!
Denominator is zero or absent
#N/A
No available match/result
#VALUE!
Wrong type in an operation
#REF!
A reference points to a deleted/invalid location
#NAME?
Excel does not recognise a name or function
Follow the cause before choosing a fallback
Case 1 has Revenue 100000 and Orders 0. =C11/D11 fails. A deliberately labelled result can use
=IF(D11=0,"Not applicable",C11/D11). But positive revenue with zero orders also needs
reconciliation: the two numbers may use different periods or populations. The label does not
resolve that inconsistency. A missing denominator must be distinguished from a confirmed zero
in new data.
Case 2 has unknown Product ID P999. Use an exact XLOOKUP with "Not Found" and record the
unresolved key. Ask the master-data owner to investigate; do not invent a product or price. Case
3 adds 1200 to the literal "text value". Recover the correct typed input from a confirmed source;
replacing it with 0 would change the calculation. Case 4 is a broken reference. Undo the
destructive edit if possible or restore the intended source and reference from your saved copy.
IFERROR(expression,fallback) catches many error types. It is useful only when the fallback is
valid for all errors it catches and the issue is still reported. =IFERROR(anything,0) can turn a
deleted price column into apparently free products.

Produce a real failure in a disposable copy
Create a temporary sheet named Error_Test. Put 5 in A1, 0 in B1 and =A1/B1 in C1. Observe the
error; then add a deliberate zero-denominator guard. Change B1 to 2 and confirm the answer
recalculates to 2.5.
Next put 10 in E1 and =E1*2 in F1. Delete column E using its column header. The dependent
formula moves left and shows #REF!. Undo to recover it. Do this only in the disposable sheet, not
in source data. Save before/after evidence and a sentence describing the repair. An IFERROR
wrapper would have concealed the damage without restoring the dependency.
Changed retry
With the answer closed, use 12 divided by a confirmed 0, a lookup for Department D99 from
EFA5's retry master, and a deleted reference to a cell holding 7. State three distinct responses.
For the division case, later change the denominator to 3. Your result must become 4, while the
missing department and broken reference remain separate issues. Review EFA6 only after saving
your attempt.

EFA7
Data quality controls in Excel
Watch first
1. How to create & use Drop Down lists like a PRO - Advanced Excel Tricks
Earlier package watch range: 0:00-3:58. Stop manually at each listed endpoint. Topic assignment retained; chapter
boundaries and full playback have not been reverified in this review. See dropdown creation and user guidance
before building quality controls that separate prevention from detection.
Pause to connect the demonstration to the example below. Use the printed stop time when a bounded range is
given; longer recordings remain available for reference.
Detection comes before correction
Open P-EFA7_Quality. The six records are expected to have a unique Order ID, a nonblank
Region, Status Closed or Pending, and numeric Net Sales >=0. These rules belong to this
exercise: a different business might legitimately allow negative refunds. Do not generalise the
rule without checking meaning.
A dropdown helps prevent some incorrect entry. A formula check detects records already
present. Neither proves the data accurately describes the real world. A reconciliation compares
your result with a separately established total for the same population; no trusted external total
is supplied here.
Build visible row checks
Enter the following in E11:I11, then fill through row 16. TRUE means a rule is satisfied in E/G/H,
while TRUE in F means a duplicate problem; the labels explain that difference.
E11: =LEN(TRIM(B11))>0
G11: =OR(C11="Closed",C11="Pending")
H11: =AND(ISNUMBER(D11),D11>=0)
I11: =IF(AND(E11,NOT(F11),G11,H11),"OK","Investigate")
Q004 appears twice, so both records fail uniqueness. Q003 has negative sales; zero for Q005 is
valid under this rule. A status called Complete is not in the approved list. Do not silently rename
it Closed: those words may refer to different process states.
Use column J for the action: request Region, investigate source key, confirm status mapping or
examine the negative amount. Keep the raw six records until a justified correction is known. Add
a small issue summary below row 25, distinguishing the number of flags from the number of
affected records: one record may fail several rules.
Add and test an input control
Use the blank cells L11:L15 as a proposed Status entry area. Select them, Data > Data Validation
> Allow: List, Source: Closed,Pending. Enable an error alert with Stop style. Try typing Complete
and observe the response, then enter Closed. Locale separators may differ. This does not
retroactively repair C11:C16, and pasted data can bypass some entry controls, so retain
detection formulas.

Independent quality case
Retry_Data!A42:H46 contains four customer records. Check required Email (presence only),
unique Customer ID, Region in East/West/North/South and numeric Lifetime Value >=0. Put the
issue explanation in E:H or adjacent blank columns without overwriting A:D. A nonblank email is
not automatically a valid or deliverable address. Count issue flags and affected records
separately.
After review, the owner supplies the missing email; record that repair in a new attempt.
Recompute the remaining flags without deleting either duplicate. Explain which issues still
prevent a trustworthy customer total. You are ready when your checks remain correct after a
changed value, not just on the original example.

EFA8
PivotTables that answer a business
question
Watch first
1. Excel Pivot Tables - Master Data Analysis in just 45 minutes
Earlier package watch range: 0:51-15:01. Stop manually at each listed endpoint. Topic assignment retained; chapter
boundaries and full playback have not been reverified in this review. See PivotTable fields, aggregation and layout
before building live Pivots on Pivot_Source.
Pause to connect the demonstration to the example below. Use the printed stop time when a bounded range is
given; longer recordings remain available for reference.
Records become groups
Open Pivot_Source. A5:H89 contains 84 calls with one row per Call ID. Each call has a Customer,
Representative, Issue Type, Channel, Satisfaction score and fictional INR Value. A PivotTable
groups these source records and performs an aggregation, such as Count, Sum or Average. It is a
saved summary object that needs refreshing after source changes.
Rows determines the labels you group by. Columns splits those groups across the page. Values
specifies the calculation. Filters restrict the population. These choices define what one result row
means; a tidy display cannot choose the business meaning for you.
Follow with me: calls by customer
1. Select exactly Pivot_Source!A5:H89, then Insert > Table (or Ctrl+T), with headers checked. In
Table Design rename it CallData. Do not include the title or instructions above row 5.
2. Click in CallData, Insert > PivotTable > From Table/Range. Choose Existing Worksheet and
My_Pivots!A9. The earlier instructions occupy rows 1-6; do not place a Pivot over them.
3. In the field list drag Customer into Rows and Call ID into Values. Open Value Field Settings and
confirm Count, not Sum. Every ID is nonblank, so this count equals the number of source calls in
each group.
4. Compare the grand total with =COUNTA(Pivot_Source!A6:A89) in an unused check cell. It
should be 84. Each of the six customers has 14 calls. List Cedar's IDs separately if you need a
manual group check.
Create two more live Pivots with room to expand: My_Pivots!A25 for Average Satisfaction by
Representative and A41 for Sum of Value by Issue Type. Change Value Field Settings explicitly.
Show satisfaction to two decimals; it is a score out of five, not a percentage. For Value, use a
currency/number format with an INR label. Sum of all Value is 345666.

Do a new question yourself
In My_Pivots!A57 build Sum of Value with Channel in Rows and Representative in Columns.
Identify the highest-value Channel and reconcile its total to source. A count of Value would
answer how many numeric values exist, not their sum. If Values defaults to Count unexpectedly,
inspect types, then select the aggregation the question requires.
A refresh test with evidence
Save a baseline copy. In a separate retry copy, append this record immediately below CallData,
checking that the Table expands to include row 90:
Field
New value
Call ID / Date
Customer / Representative
Cedar / Asha
Issue Type / Channel
Billing / Email
Satisfaction / Value
Before refreshing, record whether the Pivot is stale. Right-click each Pivot > Refresh, or use Data
> Refresh All. Confirm the count increases by one and Value by 1000, with matching group
changes. If it does not, inspect the source Table's range before recreating the Pivot. Keep the
retry copy; return to the original 84-record copy for EFA9 so expected results align. Review the
protected answer after your saved attempt.

EFA9
PivotCharts, slicers and honest
report design
Watch first
1. Excel Pivot Tables - Master Data Analysis in just 45 minutes
Earlier package watch range: 20:32-24:40. Stop manually at each listed endpoint. Topic assignment retained;
chapter boundaries and full playback have not been reverified in this review. See PivotChart/slicer reporting
patterns before building My_Report and testing filter/clear states.
Pause to connect the demonstration to the example below. Use the printed stop time when a bounded range is
given; longer recordings remain available for reference.
Make the question visible
Use the original 84-call data from EFA8. Your first chart asks how call counts change by month in
the supplied extract. It does not establish the workload of the whole company: January starts on
the 2nd and March ends on the 26th, so these are unequal partial coverage periods.
A PivotChart displays a PivotTable's summary. A slicer is a visible filter with buttons. Its Report
Connections determine which compatible Pivots it controls. Selecting a slicer button is not useful
unless you can explain which records were included.
Follow with me
1. Create a PivotTable from CallData at My_Report!A9. Put Call Date in Rows and Call ID in Values
as Count.
